title: Scripps unites television operations under Dean Littleton’s leadership
summary: CINCINNATI – The E.W. Scripps Company (NASDAQ: SSP) has promoted veteran television leader Dean Littleton to president of media, combining leadership of the company’s enterprise television and broadcast operations under Littleton in a newly created role for the company.
body_text: Scripps unites television operations under Dean Littleton’s leadership July 22, 2026 By Rebecca McCarter CINCINNATI – The E.W. Scripps Company (NASDAQ: SSP) has promoted veteran television leader Dean Littleton to president of media, combining leadership of the company’s enterprise television and broadcast operations under Littleton in a newly created role for the company. Littleton will oversee Scripps’ complete television business: its local media portfolio of approximately 60 TV stations, its national Scripps Networks division – including ION and the company’s portfolio of multicast and digital networks – and Scripps News, the company’s 24/7 national streaming news service. The organizational realignment brings Scripps Networks under Littleton’s purview, uniting Scripps’ local and national television operations to capture growth and efficiency opportunities in an increasingly fluid media landscape. Dean Littleton Littleton previously served as executive vice president of media broadcast operations and senior vice president of local media after joining Scripps in 2017 as general manager of KMGH Denver7 and KCDO The Spot – Scripps’ ABC affiliate and independent TV stations in Denver. “Dean has been instrumental in driving operational excellence across our local media platform while creating a more durable and sustainable business model for local journalism,” said Scripps President and CEO Adam Symson. “As Scripps executes its transformation plan, Dean is the right mission-focused leader to ensure our media businesses operate with the speed, creativity and growth mindset that will create lasting value for the audiences, advertisers, employees and shareholders we serve.” Before joining Scripps, Littleton held leadership roles at local television stations in Knoxville and Denver, including general manager at WATE-TV and general sales manager positions at WVLT-TV, KUSA-TV and WBIR-TV. He began his career as a news photographer and editor. “Scripps has built one of the most powerful video distribution platforms in the country, and we have a strong opportunity to steer the evolution of video-led media by staying focused on what matters most – connecting communities across the country with essential news, weather, sports and entertainment from brands they trust,” said Littleton. “I’m honored to lead our talented teams who are dedicated to our mission of creating connection for audiences across every platform, and I’m committed to building on the strong foundation we’ve established to drive growth and innovation across our local and national brands.” Littleton serves as immediate past chair of the ABC Affiliate Board of Governors and the Colorado Broadcasters Association. He is a graduate of the University of Tennessee. He will be based in Cincinnati. Investor contact: Carolyn Micheli, The E.W. Scripps Company, (513) 977-3732, [email protected] Media contact: Becca McCarter, The E.W. Scripps Company, (513) 410-2425, [email protected] About Scripps The E.W. Scripps Company (NASDAQ: SSP) is a diversified media company focused on creating connection. As one of the nation’s largest local TV broadcasters, Scripps serves communities with quality, objective local journalism and operates a portfolio of about 60 stations in 40 markets. Scripps reaches households across the U.S. with national news outlet Scripps News and popular entertainment brands ION, Bounce, Grit, ION Mystery, ION Plus and Laff. Scripps is the nation’s largest holder of broadcast spectrum. Scripps Sports serves professional and college sports leagues, conferences and teams with local market depth and national broadcast reach of up to 100% of TV households. Founded in 1878, Scripps is the steward of the Scripps National Spelling Bee, and its longtime motto is: “Give light and the people will find their own way.” Scripps in the news Scripps press releases

title: Garmin unveils G2000 PRIME Integrated Flight Deck
summary: Garmin today introduced G2000® PRIME, its new premium integrated flight deck for high-performance Class I/II piston and electric aircraft.
body_text: OLATHE, Kan./July 16, 2026/PR Newswire – Garmin (NYSE: GRMN) today introduced G2000® PRIME , its new premium integrated flight deck for high-performance Class I/II piston and electric aircraft. Leveraging innovations debuted in the G3000 PRIME flight deck, G2000 PRIME refines the flight deck experience for another class of aircraft with sleek, intuitive, all-touchscreen displays. State-of-the-art user interface design and advanced connectivity enable G2000 PRIME to leverage cutting-edge technologies that can enhance safety potential and efficiency while minimizing pilot workload in every phase of flight.“ The response to our PRIME flight decks has been incredibly enthusiastic, and we’re excited to bring this next-generation technology to high-performance light general aviation aircraft with G2000 PRIME. As pilots and aircraft manufacturers continue to seek more intuitive, capable and connected avionics, G2000 PRIME delivers on that demand with a premium flight deck experience designed to help simplify operations, enhance situational awareness and support advanced safety-enhancing technologies. It represents an important step forward in bringing Garmin’s most advanced integrated flight deck innovations to more aircraft and more pilots.” –Phil Straub, Garmin Executive Vice President and Managing Director, Aviation Stunning edge-to-edge glass flight displays G2000 PRIME features expansive 14-inch touchscreen primary display units (PDU) with edge-to-edge, sunlight-readable, fingerprint-resistant glass, redefining expectations in cockpit aesthetics and functionality. The vibrant displays include multiple performance enhancements such as quadruple the memory and gigabit system connectivity that is up to 100 times faster than earlier systems. New, faster multi-core processors more than double the processing power – leveraging Garmin’s experience certifying multi-core technology for civil and military aviation markets as early as 2017. Additionally, higher display refresh rates provide crisp, smooth animations and an impressively responsive and fluid experience. The secondary display units (SDU) provide data entry and system control, with the added capability to display multi-function applications. The high-resolution, 7-inch SDUs boast a 40% increase in screen area over prior Garmin touch controllers. Additionally, in certain aircraft applications, the SDUs can double as an integrated standby flight instrument display, removing the need for a dedicated standby flight instrument in the panel. G2000 PRIME’s new advanced multi-touch touchscreen interface, capable of recognizing up to 10 touchscreen inputs at once, allows both pilot and copilot to interact with the same display simultaneously. The enhanced multi-touch technology also enables on-screen hand stabilization, allowing pilots to give precise touchscreen inputs while simultaneously resting their fingers on the display. Modern & intuitive new user interface G2000 PRIME boasts a modern, yet familiar user interface, blending Garmin’s rich experience in avionics design with a sleek, contemporary look and feel. Enhanced fonts and iconography ensure clarity and familiarity, while smartly organized and shallow application menus provide quick access to critical functions. Primary Flight Windows (PFW) and Multi-Function Windows (MFW) maximize situational awareness with full-screen or split-screen options. New quick access bars allow pilots to open common apps such as maps, traffic, weather and charts with one touch. While viewing maps, pilots can touch anywhere to open a radial menu with options for accessing additional airport, weather, or airspace information, or quickly adjusting a flight plan via graphical editing. Interactive engine and electrical indications allow pilots to quickly open systems controls and information such as cabin environmental controls, synoptics and more. To further ease information management, the Window Manager feature allows pilots to configure app display, window sizing, and more across the entire flight deck from one SDU. The Window Manager also provides multiple preset options that can configure all displays with one command, eliminating the need for operators to manually configure each window for various phases of flight. Advanced flight tools G2000 PRIME provides enhanced flight management system (FMS) tools like the Modified Flight Plan, which allows pilots to use both the PDU and SDUs to provide a side-by-side graphical preview of flight plan changes, including performance calculation comparisons or what-if scenarios. During initialization, pilots can also elect to set up an Emergency Return function, which simplifies pilot responses to in-flight emergencies shortly after takeoff. Recently introduced to Garmin integrated flight decks, Taxiway Routing has been further improved to provide automated route guidance on the 2D navigational maps and 3D Synthetic Vision Technology (SVT™) depictions. G2000 PRIME provides advanced automation with smart checklists that are linked to crew alerting system (CAS) messages. When pilots receive a CAS message that is associated with a checklist, pilots may simply tap the message to open the appropriate checklist with a single touch. The checklists can also now sense indications and show within the checklist that the item is in the correct position, value or configuration – or provide pilots with the option to quickly view detailed synoptics. Integration with Garmin-designed Electronic Power Distribution Systems replaces traditional switches with intuitive electronic circuit breakers, providing enhanced automation and ensuring a streamlined and modern cockpit experience. Unmatched safety-enhancing innovations G2000 PRIME features a wide array of industry-leading advanced safety-enhancing technologies available only from Garmin, including Autonomí, Garmin’s family of autonomous safety-enhancing technologies. Collier Trophy recipient, Garmin Autoland, can take complete control of the flight to land the aircraft in an emergency situation where the pilot is unable to do so1. Additional safety tools such as Smart Glide™, Smart Rudder Bias, Electronic Stability Protection (ESP™), Emergency Descent Mode (EDM) and Garmin Autothrottle further ensure confidence in every flight. Garmin’s terminal safety solutions add even more capabilities to G2000 PRIME-equipped aircraft. Award-winning Runway Occupancy Awareness (ROA) technology analyzes GPS and ADS-B traffic information relevant to the airport’s runways and taxiways to assess and alert the flight crew of a possible runway incursion or collision. ROA builds upon Garmin’s other terminal safety solutions including 3D SafeTaxi® and Garmin SurfaceWatch™. Seamless connectivity and integration Stay fully connected while flying behind G2000 PRIME using a variety of supported connectivity options such as Connext Satellite Services, LTE, SiriusXM, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth® and more. Garmin’s PlaneSync™ connected aircraft management system automatically updates databases2, logs flight and engine data and allows aircraft owners and operators to remotely check fuel and systems status via the Garmin Pilot™ app3. Automated cockpit functions such as flight plan uploads over PlaneSync ensure pilots have access to real-time data, enhancing their operational efficiency and decision-making. Initial aircraft delivering with G2000 PRIME will be announced by aircraft manufacturers. To learn more, visit Garmin.com/G2000PRIME . Garmin products and services have revolutionized flight and become essential to the lives of pilots and aircraft owners and operators around the world. A leading provider of solutions to general aviation, business aviation, rotorcraft, advanced air mobility, government and defense, and commercial air carrier customers, Garmin believes every day is an opportunity to innovate. Recipient of the prestigious Robert J. Collier Trophy for Garmin Autoland , Garmin developed the world’s first certified autonomous system that activates during an emergency to control and land an aircraft without human intervention. Visit the Garmin Newsroom , email our media team , connect with @garminaviation on social, or follow our blog . 1 See Garmin.com/ALuse for Autoland system requirements and limitations. 2 Active PlaneSync and database subscriptions required for automatic database updates. Active PlaneSync subscription plan required for flight log uploading. Features are available on-ground only and requires GDL 60 to have active LTE or Wi-Fi connectivity; signal strength and other factors may apply. See Garmin.com/PlaneSyncCoverage for LTE coverage details. 3 Remote aircraft status requires active PlaneSync subscription. User’s smart device must have internet connectivity. Feature is available on-ground only and requires GDL 60 to have LTE connectivity; signal strength and other factors may apply. See Garmin.com/PlaneSyncCoverage for coverage details. ###

title: Bid Bonds: An All-in-One Guide
summary: Bid bonds are a type of surety bond that is required by project owners during the bidding process for construction projects. They guarantee that the bidder has the financial stability and capabilities to complete the project as required. Read this comprehensive guide to learn all about bid bonds.
body_text: Whether you’re an owner or a contractor, if you are planning on taking on a new project and want to take all of the necessary steps to protect yourself financially, obtaining a bid bond will definitely be on your to do list. In this article, we’ll answer your questions about bid bonds, including what they are, why you need them, and how to get one. We’ll also guide you through the ins and outs of what to look out for when obtaining a bid bond. Surety Bond Basics A surety bond is a three party contract in which one party, the surety, guarantees a second party, the obligee, the successful performance of a third party, the principal. The purpose of a surety bond is to protect public and private interest against financial loss, by both weeding out potentially unqualified obligees and acting as insurance against any unforeseen losses. What are the different types of surety bonds? While there are many diverse and niche surety bonds for different situations, there are generally four main categories of surety bonds: contract surety bonds, judicial surety bonds, probate court surety bonds, and commercial surety bonds. These four types of surety bonds all serve different functions and are purchased for different purposes. Contract surety bonds The purpose of contract bonds is to incentivize the obligee to agree to a contract with the principal. Sometimes referred to as construction bonds, these bonds are commonly used in the construction industry. Common types of contract surety bonds include bid bonds, performance bonds, payment bonds, supply bonds, maintenance bonds, and improvement bonds required by municipalities. Judicial surety bonds Judicial surety bonds are used in court proceedings and are categorized into bail bonds, appeal bonds, mechanic's lien bonds, attachment bonds, and injunction bonds. Probate court surety bonds Probate court surety bonds guarantee that appointed trustees, guardians, executors, or administrators will act with honesty, loyalty, and good faith towards beneficiaries. For example, a probate court surety bond could be used to guarantee that the trustee of a recently deceased individual will, in good faith, distribute the assets of the deceased, or in other cases, serve as a legal guardian to the decedent's child. Commercial Surety Bonds Commercial surety bonds are an umbrella category, covering a range of bonds that do not fall under the other three categories. License and permit bonds are required by governments for various licenses and permits, while public official bonds may be required for certain public officials. Business service bonds protect business clients from employee actions, while fidelity bonds protect companies and clients against employee embezzlement. Other common types of surety bonds may be used for lost promissory notes, self-insurance, and commercial leases. What are bid bonds? A bid bond is a type of surety bond that is typically required during the bidding process for construction projects. It is a form of guarantee that assures the project owner that the bidder will enter into the contract and provide the required performance bond and payment bond if they are awarded the project. Bid bonds are a crucial aspect of the construction bidding process. Also known as bid security, they provide assurance to the project owner that the bidder has the capability and financial stability to complete the work as per the contractual agreement. In this article, we will go in-depth about how bid bonds work, their significance in the construction industry, and how they benefit both the project owner and bidder. How do Bid Bonds Work? During the bidding process, all potential bidders must provide bid bonds to demonstrate their commitment to the project. Bid bonds guarantee the owner that the bidder has the financial resources and abilities to complete the project as required. In the event that the lowest bidder fails to execute a contract and withdraws from a project for which they provided a bid bond, the owner of the project may file a bid bond claim against both the bidder and their surety company. Bid bond claims help the owner obtain compensation for the difference in cost it may take to secure the services of the next lowest bidder. This means that if the previous bidder offered a proposal for $100,000 and the next lowest competitor bid was $110,000, the forfeiting bidder may be responsible for the $10,000 difference between the bids, up to the amount of the bond they put up as a guarantee. If the forfeiting bidder does not pay the claim amount and any related attorney fees, they may be pursued by their bid bond company. It is recommended to carefully review your bid bond form beforehand to fully understand the level of liability exposure. Bid bonds are typically issued by a surety bond company, which is a third-party organization that assumes the risks associated with the bond. The surety company evaluates the financial stability and capabilities of the bidder through a thorough evaluation process. Once the surety provider approves the bond, the bidder pays a premium for the bond which is typically a percentage of the total project amount. Why are Bid Bonds important? Bid bonds are crucial in the construction industry because they protect the project owner from financial losses due to a bidder's default. A construction Bid bond guarantees that the bidder has the financial stability, experience, and capabilities to perform the work as required and will not back out of the project. If a bidder fails to complete the work, the bid bond amount will be forfeited to the project owner, allowing them to find a new bidder and complete the project without additional costs. Moreover, bid bonds encourage bidders to estimate their costs accurately and thoroughly evaluate the project requirements before bidding. It also ensures that all bidders have an equal opportunity to bid on the project without compromising the project's quality. Who Needs a Bid Bond? This type of bond is required by both government departments and general contractors. The bond is needed in contracts involving public construction projects. While sometimes optional for private projects, bid bonds are required by law for public, government sanctioned contractor jobs because they involve taxpayer money and either federal, state, or local jurisdiction. In many cases, if you fail to file the required bond, your bid will automatically be disqualified from the bidding process. In specific cases where they are allowed, there are a few alternatives for bid bonds, such as cashier’s checks, certified checks, money orders, or other liquid assets that a contractor can put down as a promise that they will follow through on their contract. Benefits of a Bid Bond Bid bonds offer numerous benefits to project owners, as well as offering benefits to the bidder. Benefits for Project Owner Provides financial security throughout the bidding process. If a bidder fails to follow through the project or goes bankrupt, the project owner will receive compensation through the bid security Allows project owners to evaluate bidders' financial resources and abilities to assess if they can carry out the project requirements Discourages frivolous bidding and ensures that the project owner receives a reasonable and accurate bid. Benefits for Contractor Bidder Encourages bidders to make more extensive bids and provide more reliable estimates since they guarantee that all bidders will only bid on projects that they can complete fully Project owners will be more assured in projects and more likely to proceed, giving bidders more opportunity for work and perform accordingly Provides a boost to their financial credibility as they have been evaluated by a surety agency How are Bid Bonds Different From Other Similar Bonds? Bid bonds and performance bonds are two different types of bonds used in the construction industry. Both are required by project owners to ensure that the contractor completes the project according to the terms of the contract. However, there are several differences between these two types of bonds. Bid bonds vs. Performance bonds Similarities: Both bid bonds and performance bonds serve as guarantees that the contractor will fulfill their obligations as outlined in the bid bond form. Both types of bonds are issued by a surety agency or insurance company. Both require the contractor to pay a premium for the bond. Both may require collateral or an indemnity agreement. Differences: Purpose: A bid bond is issued to guarantee that the contractor will enter into a contract if they are awarded the project. Performance bonds, on the other hand, guarantee that the contractor will complete the project according to the contract. Timing: Bid bonds are required during the bidding process, while performance bonds are required after a contract has been awarded. Cost: Bid bonds typically cost less than performance bonds as they are seen as less risky. Coverage: Bid bonds cover only the bid amount, while performance bonds cover the entire contract price. Liability: If the contractor defaults on their obligations, the liability for the bid bond falls on the surety or insurance company, while the liability for performance bonds falls on the contractor. Bid bonds are usually replaced with performance bonds once the contract has been awarded and signed. This is because the performance bond covers the same obligations as the bid bond, but with the added assurance that the contractor will complete the project. In some cases, both bid and performance bonds may be required for a project, in which case they will be in effect simultaneously. Bid bonds and performance bonds, what's the difference ? Check here to find out! How do I Get a Bid Bond? The process of getting a bid bond usually involves the following steps: Find a surety broker. A surety broker is a licensed professional who represents multiple surety companies and can help contractors find the best bond for their needs. Complete a bond application. A bid bond request will usually include information about the project, the contractor's experience and financial status, and other relevant information. Underwriting. After the application is submitted, the bid bond company (the surety) will evaluate the contractor's creditworthiness and likelihood of fulfilling the terms of the contract. Bond issuance. If the contractor meets the surety company's requirements, the surety will issue the bid bond, typically for a percentage of the total contract amount. Requirements for a Bid Bond To get a bid bond, contractors must meet certain requirements set by the surety company providing the bond. Construction Bid bond requirements typically include the following: Proof of financial stability Good credit history Record of successful completion of past construction projects Surety companies will also evaluate a contractor's experience, skillset, and reputation when determining whether to issue a bond. Where to Get a Bid Bond? The first step of getting a bid bond is finding a surety broker is an essential and important step to get right when seeking a bid bond. When choosing a surety broker, it's important to consider factors such as reputation, experience, and customer service. A good broker should be knowledgeable about the bond market and able to provide guidance on the best bond for a contractor's needs. It's also important to work with a broker who is responsive and committed to providing excellent customer service. SuretyNow has experts licensed in all 50 states on hand to answer questions 24/7—contact us if you need help with looking for a bid bond! How Much do Bid Bonds Cost? The cost of a bid bond varies depending on factors such as the size of the contract and the contractor's creditworthiness. Like other surety bonds, the price one pays depends on the bond amount—which is the size of the contract—and the premium rate—determined by the contractor's credit and financial history. As always, the price will be the bond amount multiplied by the premium rate. Price you pay = Bond Amount * Premium Rate The bond amount for a bid bond is the dollar amount of the contract project bid price. For example, if the project would cost $100,000 to complete by the contractor, the bid bond guarantee amount would be set at $100,000. Typically, the premium rate for bid bonds can be between 1% and 5% of the total contract amount, although the premium can be up to 10%. Contractors with stronger financials and credit histories may be able to obtain lower rates, while those with weaker financials may pay more. After the lowest bidding contractor wins the bid, the bid bond is replaced by a performance bond (sometimes along with other construction bonds). Performance bonds are usually priced with a premium rate of 3% of the bond amount. Conclusion Bid bonds are a crucial aspect of the construction industry, providing financial security, promoting competition, and ensuring project owners that the bidder has the financial capabilities and experience to complete the project requirements. They benefit both the project owner and bidder by providing credibility, financial stability, and protection against losses. To ensure that your bidding process runs smoothly, please feel free to contact us to get started on obtaining your bid bond.

title: Karman Expands International
summary: Karman announced an agreement to acquire Glasgow-headquartered Walker Precision Engineering (“Walker”) for total consideration of approximately $94 million or £70 million. Upon closing, Karman expects the acquisition to expand access to current and next-generation European and other allied nation missile programs.
body_text: Karman’s strategy is to deliver advanced systems and subsystems for high-growth end markets, serving the United States and its allies’ highest priority national security interests, from deep sea to deep space Through integrated design, IP protected products and vertical integration, Karman is architected for agility and speed, delivering the best technology for the most challenging environments The planned acquisition of Walker Precision Engineering significantly advances this strategy and further aligns Karman’s business with core national and allied security priorities FARNBOROUGH, England–( BUSINESS WIRE )–Farnborough Airshow — Karman Space & Defense (“Karman”, “Karman Holdings, Inc.” or “the Company”) (NYSE: KRMN), a leader in the rapid design, development, and production of critical, next-generation systems that align with the core mission priorities of the U.S. Department of War and its allies, and meet the accelerating demand for access to space, today announced an agreement to acquire Glasgow-headquartered Walker Precision Engineering (“Walker”) for total consideration of approximately $94 million or £70 million. Walker possesses unique, integrated manufacturing capabilities that span engineering, advanced materials design, precision machining, electroplating and electromechanical assemblies. Walker’s advanced products support missile seekers, guidance systems and control systems on more than 25 EU tactical missile, air and defense programs for prime contractors whose reach extends around the globe. The acquisition accelerates Karman’s expansion beyond the United States, providing a European footprint from which to add to its 17 locations across eight U.S. states. Walker’s customers, advanced IP and technology represent a highly complementary fit with Karman’s, providing the combined customer base with an enhanced set of solutions to solve mission-critical challenges. “Karman continues to invest in the capacity and capabilities that will help our customers deliver on an unprecedented wave of end market demand,” said Jon Rambeau, Karman chief executive officer. “We expect that Walker’s strong missile- and aviation-related capabilities and programmatic relationships with the largest European space and defense prime contractors will increase our addressable market and create new opportunities for development, cross-selling and export, across our enterprise. We look forward to welcoming the talented Walker employees in Scotland, England and Poland to the Karman team. “By focusing on high priority missions and by delivering strong, consistent performance, Walker has built a robust growth pipeline. We believe that operating as part of Karman will unlock valuable synergies that will broaden that pipeline to maximize long-term prospects for growth,” Mr. Rambeau added. “Over the past eight years, Walker has invested in our people, facilities and capabilities to become a trusted manufacturing partner to industry leaders across the aerospace, defense and space sectors,” said George Adams, Walker chief executive officer. “Joining Karman marks an exciting new chapter that will allow us to build on those foundations.” Since its inception in 1979, Walker has established multi-decade relationships with top global defense primes, developing a vertically integrated, one-stop shop capable of performing all critical processes in-house. The transaction is expected to close during the third quarter of Karman’s fiscal year 2026, subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals. Upon closing, Karman expects the acquisition to expand access to current and next-generation European and other allied nation missile programs. The acquisition is also expected to be immediately accretive to Karman revenue, backlog, adjusted EBITDA, adjusted earnings per share and cash flow. ADVISORS Kroll acted as exclusive sell-side advisor to Walker Precision Engineering and shareholders, providing Investment Banking services. ABOUT KARMAN SPACE & DEFENSE Karman Space & Defense is a leader in the rapid design, development and production of critical, next-generation system solutions that align with the U.S. Department of War’s core mission priorities and the nation’s accelerating demand for access to space. Building on nearly 50 years of success, we deliver Payload & Protection Systems, Hydro/Aerodynamic Interstage Systems, and Propulsion & Launch Systems to over 80 prime contractors supporting more than 130 space and defense programs. Karman is headquartered in Huntington Beach, Calif., with multiple facilities across the United States. title: State Chief Privacy Officers Can Have Real Power
summary: Utah has given its CPO a meaningful role — and he has thoughts on how other states should follow
body_text: Back to News & Commentary State Chief Privacy Officers Can Have Real Power Utah has given its CPO a meaningful role — and he has thoughts on how other states should follow Jay Stanley , ACLU Speech, Privacy, and Technology Project Share This Page July 22, 2026 Subscribe to the Free Future Newsletter Or get immediate notifications of new posts via Substack Free Future home I’ve been writing in recent months about how digital identity systems are potentially disastrous for privacy and how the state of Utah is being uniquely thoughtful in its approach to the technology. But Utah seems to be taking an interesting approach to privacy in ways that go beyond the digital ID issue. An example is the role it has created for a state chief privacy officer (CPO). Though Utah is not always good on privacy — its commercial privacy law is one of the weakest in the nation, for example, and its new law targeting the use of VPNs threatens the use of that vital privacy-protecting technology nationwide. Nevertheless, Utah has long been an occasional bright spot on privacy, and its current governor, Spencer Cox, has shown genuine concern about both governmental and consumer privacy. My sense is that a lot of people in the privacy world haven’t really focused on state CPOs; I certainly haven’t. But as the ACLU has long held , privacy laws need to be backed up by institutions that enforce them or they may wither on the vine, as we have seen with laws such as the federal Privacy Act of 1974. Good privacy oversight institutions should include both independent oversight bodies (such as the California Privacy Protection Agency) and privacy officials working within government agencies. State CPOs are not independent from a state’s political leadership but with the support of such leadership can play an important role. I recently spoke to Utah’s dynamic CPO, Christopher Bramwell, and asked him about how Utah is approaching the role, how it has institutionalized privacy in general, and how that differs from most other states. He made several interesting arguments during our conversation (quotes edited for length and clarity). 1. The CPO role should be bigger than compliance First I asked Bramwell about the general role of CPOs in the states, and how many states even have CPOs. Pointing to a survey from the National Association of State Chief Information Officers that has a lot of information about the role across states, he told me: Twenty-five states have somebody in an executive privacy officer role. Some of them are “privacy analyst.” Some of them are a “privacy manager.” Some of them are just “other duties as assigned.” So it's very different what states have in terms of the formality of the role. Now, most of those, though — this is where you need to separate out Utah's approach from other states — most states are looking at privacy from a compliance perspective: “What are we required to do and are we doing it?” Not from a “What should the public policy be to have the best privacy to protect our citizens?” 2. Don’t have your CPO report to the Chief Information Officer (CIO) Utah has been very intentional about creating checks and balances around privacy. As a result, the Chief Privacy Officer serves as the director of an independent office within the Utah Department of Government Operations and does not report to the Chief Information Officer. Most CIOs are responsible for helping government modernize systems, improve service delivery, and enable the effective use of data. Those are critical responsibilities. At the same time, privacy leaders are tasked with ensuring that modernization efforts appropriately account for individual rights, transparency, accountability, and long-term public trust. This is not a criticism of CIOs or the important work they do. As government digitizes, there will inevitably be situations where competing interests must be balanced. The question isn’t whether modernization or privacy should prevail, it’s whether privacy interests are represented by an independent voice in those discussions. Utah's approach has been to create clear separation of duties so that both perspectives can be fully considered as part of the decision-making process. We work very closely with our CIO and technology leadership. Privacy is integrated into the discussion early, which creates alignment, reduces friction, and allows us to move forward with greater confidence. I report actually to a cabinet member, the head of the Department of Government Operations. He’s also the chair of the Utah Privacy Governing Board, which is made up of the five highest elected officials in the state or their designees. 3. Institutionalize privacy beyond just one office or officer Utah is one of only a handful of states where the Chief Privacy Officer is established in statute and it's actually a governor-appointed position. So having statutory duties and being appointed by the governor elevates privacy from an administrative function to a matter of statewide public policy and governance. We also have the Government Data Privacy Act , which I believe may be the most comprehensive state government privacy law in the country governing how governmental entities process personal data. More importantly, Utah has made sure not to rely on a single office or individual to advance privacy. We’ve intentionally built a broader governance framework that includes the Office of Data Privacy, the Utah Privacy Governing Board, and an independent privacy audit function within the Office of the State Auditor. There’s also our Utah Privacy Commission, which is an independent advisory body composed of public employees and private citizens appointed by the Governor, Attorney General, and State Auditor. Its role is to study emerging privacy issues and provide policy recommendations. My role exists within that larger framework. The objective is not simply to assess compliance, but to help implement a long-term statewide privacy strategy to steadily increase privacy maturity across government over the course of a decade. 4. Getting privacy fundamentals right is vital in the age of AI and big tech The privacy challenges facing governments today are fundamentally different from those of even a decade ago. Advances in artificial intelligence, surveillance technologies, large-scale data collection, and digital identity systems are creating new opportunities, but also new risks that many existing governance frameworks were never designed to address. There will be growing pressure to automate decisions and optimize outcomes, but those objectives have to be be balanced against transparency, accountability, and an individual's ability to make informed choices about their own life. That concern drives much of the work we are doing in Utah. States need more than isolated privacy requirements — they need comprehensive privacy strategies that can adapt to these rapidly evolving technologies. 5. Many states are ignoring key aspects of their privacy laws Most states adopted records management and retention laws in the sixties and seventies. As governments modernized, many replaced paper processes with digital technologies but never fully adapted those systems to comply with those laws. The result is that many systems were built to retain data indefinitely, even where laws require it to be disposed of. One of the foundational questions states should be asking is whether their data governance practices have kept pace with their technology modernization efforts. In many cases, they have not. Last year, we conducted research across all 50 states to identify generally applicable laws and policies related to key data governance practices. We compiled the results into a publicly available spreadsheet that allows users to navigate directly to the applicable laws in each state. The purpose was to make these requirements more accessible and transparent. In many cases, policymakers, researchers, journalists, and members of the public don’t even know what questions to ask or what legal requirements already exist. Our resource is intended to help states assess where they stand today, identify gaps in their governance frameworks, and ask important questions about whether existing laws are being enforced. 6. All the agencies and local governments in a state can't do privacy right without help One of the most important roles a Chief Privacy Officer can play is helping governmental entities in the state understand not just what privacy requirements exist, but how to systematically implement them over time. We have a statewide privacy framework — 24 practices that all Utah government entities are supposed to comply with. We actually lay out, here's the high-level strategy for the state, and here are the practices that you should be implementing. That means: Who's accountable, who should be doing the work? How do you do transparency? How do you give notice? How do you ensure individuals have access to their data? Meaningful privacy modernization doesn’t happen overnight. Most states will require years of sustained effort to build mature privacy programs across hundreds or thousands of governmental entities. We use a maturity model to help entities assess where they are today and identify practical steps for improvement. State law also requires annual reporting on privacy program maturity and planned improvements. The goal is to create a cycle of assessment, planning, and implementation that steadily increases privacy maturity across government over time. 7. Political support is crucial None of this would be possible without support from elected leadership. One of the reasons Utah has been able to move quickly is that privacy has been recognized as a strategic issue that deserves attention at the highest levels of government. Governor Cox has been a strong advocate for privacy, issuing a statewide privacy executive order, supporting the creation of the Office of Data Privacy, and helping advance broader discussions around digital identity and his pro-human AI approach. We have also worked closely with the Legislature. Members of both the House and Senate participate in the Utah Privacy Governing Board, which helps make sure privacy priorities remain aligned across branches of government. I’m not enough of an expert on state government and privacy governance to have informed opinions on all these details, but based on what I’ve seen from Bramwell in the digital ID arena in which I do work, his views are very much worth considering. title: The best AI SDR for Salesforce users in 2026
summary: The AI SDRs that integrate deepest with Salesforce, ranked by native sync, owner mapping, DNC control, and pipeline reporting, with honest verdicts.
body_text: The best AI sales development representative (SDR) for Salesforce users is Artisan. Ava runs outbound end to end and treats Salesforce as the source of truth, with native bidirectional sync, dynamic lists and report imports as campaign sources, owner mapping, CRM-driven do-not-contact, and pipeline-influenced reporting. Salesforce's own Agentforce SDR, Regie, and Apollo are worth considering too, depending on your stack. If your revenue org already runs on Salesforce, the AI SDR you pick lives or dies by how honestly it respects the CRM. A tool that dumps unqualified contacts, ignores account ownership, or emails a company you have an open deal with will cost you more trust than it earns pipeline. This guide ranks the options by Salesforce depth, not brand size, and tells you who should pick each one. The best AI SDRs for Salesforce at a glance Rank Tool Best for Standout Salesforce capability Pricing 1 Artisan Teams that want Ava to run outbound with Salesforce as the source of truth Bidirectional sync, report and list imports, CRM-driven DNC, pipeline reporting Usage-based credits, no seat fee, free trial 2 Salesforce Agentforce SDR Teams committed to keeping everything inside Salesforce Native CRM residency and security posture $2/conversation or Flex Credits ($0.10/action) 3 Regie.ai Rep-augmentation teams that want enterprise sequencing on top of Salesforce Sequencer plus Auto-Pilot agents $180-499/user/month per its pricing 4 Apollo Budget-conscious teams that treat Salesforce as the system of record All-in-one data plus engagement with CRM sync Free to $119/user/month per its pricing How we chose Four criteria, weighted for Salesforce users specifically: How much of the job the AI does. Does the tool run sourcing, outreach, reply handling, and booking, or hand most of it back to your reps? Depth of native Salesforce sync. Bidirectional writes, custom objects, owner mapping, task sync, and reports and lists as live sources, not a one-way contact dump. CRM-driven governance. Can the CRM enforce do-not-contact, deal protection, and field-level export control automatically? Reporting that ties back to pipeline. Does the tool show influence on revenue inside the numbers your RevOps team already trusts? Which AI SDR integrates deepest with Salesforce? Artisan integrates deepest with Salesforce because it treats the CRM as the operating system for outbound, not a place to log activity after the fact. This difference shows up at every stage of the workflow, from how campaigns are built to how meetings route to how influence is reported. 1. Artisan: The AI BDR that runs on your Salesforce data Ava is the autonomous AI business development representative (BDR) at the center of Artisan. She finds best-fit leads across over 270M B2B contacts, enriches and ranks them, launches personalized multichannel campaigns across email, social outreach, and dialer steps, handles every reply from a knowledge base, and books meetings, as autonomous as you set her to be. For Salesforce users, the point is that she does all of this while keeping Salesforce the source of truth. The Salesforce integration is fully two-way. Artisan runs a full backfill import with a deduplication waterfall, then keeps records synced in both directions. You can use Salesforce dynamic lists and Salesforce report imports as campaign sources, so the segments your RevOps team already maintains become the audiences Ava works. These same lists and reports can serve as do-not-contact sources, and custom object support means Artisan reads the objects your org actually models its business on, not just standard leads and contacts. Ownership is respected end to end. Bidirectional owner mapping plus a sender-assignment waterfall (CRM owner first, then round-robin) means outreach goes out from the right rep's mailbox, and booked meetings land on the right calendar. Governance is CRM-driven: deal-based and domain-based do-not-contact can block everyone at a company with an active deal, configurable down to deal-associated contacts only, so Ava never cold-emails into a live opportunity. Suppression is applied before enrichment, so you do not even pay to enrich a contact you should not touch. On the write side, you keep control. Field-level export control lets you set each field to do not sync, fill if empty, or overwrite, and there is a complete export off switch if you want to keep Artisan's activity out of certain fields entirely. Human-replies-only export filtering keeps auto-replies out of your records, two-way task completion sync keeps reps and Ava aligned, status mapping and multiple source-attribution values keep reporting clean, and activities log natively on the record timeline. Finally, pipeline-influenced revenue reporting ties Ava's work back to the opportunities it helped create, in the CRM your leadership already reviews. Deployment scales to the enterprise: sales ops can run Ava centrally for large account executive (AE) teams who never log in, with a full audit trail, SOC 2 Type II compliance, and single sign-on (SSO), SAML, and role-based access on Enterprise plans. Pricing is usage-based with no platform fee and a free trial; full details at artisan.co/pricing . CookUnity's Bruno Didier, Head of B2B, put the outcome plainly: "Ava runs highly targeted outreach at a scale we could never reach with a human-only team." This ran across over 100,000 emails at roughly $45 cost per lead. Best for: any team on Salesforce, from startup to enterprise, that wants an AI to own the outbound job while the CRM stays the source of truth. Who should pick something else: teams that want reps to keep manually driving every sequence and only want a lightweight assistant should look at a copilot-style tool instead. Pricing: usage-based credits, no seat fee, free trial. See artisan.co/pricing. 2. Salesforce Agentforce SDR: Native, but young Agentforce SDR is Salesforce's own AI SDR, and its headline advantage is obvious: it lives inside Salesforce, inherits the platform's security posture, and works your existing CRM data without an external sync. For a team whose non-negotiable is that nothing leaves Salesforce, this residency is a real draw. The honest limits are just as clear. Setup is steep, the consumption pricing model is still evolving, and it is a young product. It works the contacts already in your CRM rather than sourcing net-new prospects at scale, so it is more an activation layer on existing data than a full pipeline-generation engine. Best for: Salesforce-committed teams that want their AI SDR to live entirely inside the platform and are willing to invest in setup. Who should pick something else: teams that need to source net-new contacts at scale, or want faster time to value, will go further with a platform built to prospect natively. Pricing: roughly $2 per conversation, or Flex Credits at about $0.10 per action, per Salesforce. 3. Regie.ai: Enterprise sequencing with agents on top Regie.ai (RegieOne) is an AI-native sales engagement platform that combines a sequencer, a dialer, and Auto-Pilot agents. It carries genuine enterprise credibility and a rep-augmentation philosophy: output per rep scales, and it plugs into Salesforce cleanly for teams that want structured cadences with AI assistance rather than a fully autonomous agent. The tradeoff is that reps still drive. Pipeline scales with the number of people who run sequences, not independently of headcount, so it is a productivity multiplier for a staffed team rather than a replacement for the grunt work. Best for: enterprise teams that want to augment reps with AI sequencing and calling on top of Salesforce. Who should pick something else: teams that want the AI to own the workflow end to end, so pipeline grows without adding reps, should pick an autonomous platform. Pricing: $180-499/user/month, per its pricing. 4. Apollo: The value all-rounder Apollo is the price-accessible all-in-one: a large contact database (over 230M contacts claimed), plus sequencing and assistive AI, used by over 600,000 companies (over 100,000 paying), with reported annual recurring revenue (ARR) around $200M. It syncs with Salesforce and works well as a combined data and engagement layer for teams that want reach on a budget, and its acquisition of Pocus in March 2026 added signal capability. The limits for Salesforce users are the assistive (not autonomous) AI and the per-seat model. Many enterprises end up treating Apollo as a data layer that feeds other tools rather than the system that runs outbound. Best for: budget-conscious teams that want data and engagement in one tool with Salesforce as the record of truth. Who should pick something else: teams that want an autonomous AI SDR and CRM-driven governance rather than a per-seat assistive tool. Pricing: free to $119/user/month, per its pricing. What makes a Salesforce integration "deep" versus superficial? A superficial integration writes contacts and logs activity one way. A deep integration lets the CRM drive the whole motion. The features that separate them, and that a Salesforce buyer should test in a trial: Bidirectional sync with custom objects , not just standard leads and contacts, so the tool reads the way your org actually models its business. Lists and reports as live sources , so the segments RevOps maintains become campaign audiences and suppression lists without re-building them. Owner mapping and sender assignment , so outreach comes from the right rep and meetings book on the right calendar. CRM-driven do-not-contact , including blocking accounts with active deals, so cold outreach never crosses a live opportunity. Field-level export control and an off switch , so you decide exactly what the tool writes back. Pipeline-influenced reporting , so influence shows up in the numbers leadership already reviews. Artisan does all six. Most tools do one or two. How should you choose by need and stack, not size? Route by what your motion requires and where your data lives, not by company headcount. If you want an AI to own outbound while Salesforce stays authoritative, and you need deal protection, owner mapping, and pipeline reporting, Artisan is the pick whether you are a 10-person startup or a 1,000-AE enterprise. If your absolute constraint is that no data leaves Salesforce, Agentforce SDR earns the look despite its youth. If you have a staffed team you want to make faster, Regie augments reps well. If budget and database reach lead your list, Apollo is the value option. If your CRM is HubSpot instead, see the best AI SDR for HubSpot users . What changed for Salesforce AI SDRs recently? Salesforce has been consolidating the category into Agentforce. It acquired Qualified, the premium inbound specialist behind the Piper agent, in April 2026, folding it into Agentforce, and acquired Momentum in March 2026. This gives Salesforce-native buyers more first-party AI options, though the roadmap for acquired products is still settling. Apollo acquired Pocus in March 2026 to add signal-based selling. These moves make native and near-native options more numerous, but they do not change the core question: how much of the job does the AI actually own, and how deeply does it respect your CRM? For competitor deep dives, see 11x pricing and reviews and 1mind pricing and reviews . Frequently asked questions What is the best AI SDR for Salesforce users? Artisan. Ava runs the full outbound job, from sourcing net-new contacts to booking meetings, while treating Salesforce as the source of truth. It syncs bidirectionally, imports dynamic lists and Salesforce reports as campaign and do-not-contact sources, supports custom objects, maps owners to senders, enforces deal-based do-not-contact, and reports pipeline influence inside Salesforce. Salesforce's own Agentforce SDR, Regie, and Apollo are reasonable alternatives depending on your stack. Which AI SDR integrates best with Salesforce? By depth of native integration, Artisan. It goes beyond one-way contact logging: bidirectional sync, custom objects, owner mapping with a sender-assignment waterfall, lists and reports as live campaign and suppression sources, field-level export control, two-way task sync, and pipeline-influenced reporting. Agentforce SDR is the most native option by definition since it is built by Salesforce, but it is younger and works existing CRM contacts rather than sourcing net-new at scale. Does Artisan work with Salesforce custom objects? Yes. Artisan supports custom object sync, so it reads and writes the objects your org actually models its business on, not just standard leads and contacts. Combined with dynamic list and report imports as campaign sources, owner mapping, and status mapping, this lets Artisan fit the way your Salesforce instance is already configured rather than forcing a generic contact-only model. Can an AI SDR avoid emailing accounts with open Salesforce deals? Yes, if it reads deal state from the CRM. Artisan's CRM-driven do-not-contact can block everyone at a company with an active deal, configurable down to deal-associated contacts only, and suppression is applied before enrichment so you do not pay to enrich contacts you should not touch. This protects live opportunities from cold outreach automatically, which is one of the main reasons deep CRM integration matters for outbound. Is Salesforce Agentforce SDR better than Artisan because it is native? Native residency is a genuine advantage if your hard requirement is that no data leaves Salesforce, and Agentforce SDR inherits the platform's security posture. But it is a young product with steep setup and evolving consumption pricing, and it activates existing CRM contacts rather than sourcing net-new prospects at scale. Artisan integrates deeply with Salesforce while also owning the full prospecting workflow, so for most teams it does more of the job. How much does an AI SDR for Salesforce cost? It varies by model. Artisan uses usage-based credits with no platform fee and a free trial, so you pay for work performed rather than per seat; see artisan.co/pricing. Agentforce SDR runs around $2 per conversation or Flex Credits at about $0.10 per action. Regie is $180-499/user/month, and Apollo runs free to $119/user/month, both per their pricing pages. Does Artisan report pipeline influence inside Salesforce? Yes. Artisan offers pipeline-influenced revenue reporting that ties Ava's outreach back to the opportunities it helped create, using the fields and objects your leadership already reviews. Combined with multiple source-attribution values, status mapping, and native activity logging on the record timeline, this lets RevOps measure Ava's contribution in Salesforce rather than in a separate dashboard. Where to go next If you want an AI SDR that runs outbound on your Salesforce data, see how Ava works as your AI sales agent , read the definition of an AI BDR , or go deeper on Artisan for enterprise Salesforce teams. To compare the full field, start with the best AI SDRs . For adjacent categories, see the best AI BDRs , the best AI GTM platforms , and the 15 best AI sales tools . For role tooling overviews, see SDR tools and BDR tools .

title: How to build a better beauty product photography workflow: 6 steps
summary: Master beauty product photography for e‑commerce. Get tips on prep, lighting, closeups, and retouching for realistic, high-converting images.
body_text: Lipsticks and eyeshadows don’t sell themselves—quality product images do a lot of the work. But beauty is often harder to photograph than other product categories: Reflective packaging shows every fingerprint, shade swatches must match the real product so customers build brand trust, and a single catalog can hold dozens of near-identical nudes or reds that all need to look distinct and accurate. Effective beauty product photography requires accurate shade reproduction, glare-free reflective packaging, and color consistency across the full range, all formatted to each marketplace’s specs. Doing that for one product takes effort. Doing it across a whole catalog, for every marketplace, is where most brands hit a wall. That’s the gap Photoroom’s AI product photography platform is built to close, helping you create a workflow that keeps every listing consistent and on-brand . Table of contents: Prepare your beauty products Choose AI-powered production over studio shots Carefully consider composition and shot types Maintain visual consistency Streamline post-production and editing Optimize for e‑commerce marketplaces Automate your beauty product production workflow with Photoroom Makeup products’ reflective, glossy packaging tends to pick up fingerprints and dust. So before you begin shooting, wipe down each product carefully. Wearing gloves while handling the items avoids additional smudges, saving you time during the editing phase . For brands photographing entire cosmetic product lines, swatch and shade consistency is vital. When you shoot makeup swatches under inconsistent lighting or on shifting backgrounds, the colors can appear misleading, eroding customer trust and driving returns. To avoid this problem, use the same lighting and background for every makeup product photo. 2. Choose AI-powered production over studio shots A traditional beauty product photoshoot requires resources and expertise that many brands just don’t have. At a minimum, you need: A digital single-lens reflex or mirrorless camera that lets you shoot at ISO 100 A tripod for consistent framing Lighting control to reduce glare and manage shadows, typically by using softboxes or a key light, fill light, and reflector That’s just for simple, static shots; for lifestyle product staging , you’ll need additional props and equipment. And when you’re working across thousands of SKUs, this traditional studio route becomes expensive, slows down turnaround times, and makes it difficult to achieve consistency. This has pushed more beauty brands to consider AI product photography tools. Instead of building out a studio setup for every launch, you can produce visuals from existing images, text prompts, or brand assets. For example, with Photoroom, you can upload an image or explain what you want, and our platform generates high-quality listing visuals , using tools like the AI Product Fixer and Brand Kit to preserve your product fidelity . 3. Carefully consider composition and shot types The angles and shots you use in creative product photography for makeup and other beauty products shape how customers perceive those cosmetics. For this category specifically, composition determines whether things like shade and packaging details come through in the image. This affects whether items look accurate on product detail pages or in marketplace listings . For example: A hero shot of a lipstick standing upright showcases its form and packaging. A flat lay of an eyeshadow palette or a selection of blush swatches shows a full shade range in one frame. Macro photography (extreme close-ups) showcases finish and texture accuracy, along with visible qualities like shimmer particles. On-model or swatch-on-skin shots show how a shade or finish performs. Packaging or detail shots capture the product name, shade name, and finish, helping buyers compare before purchasing. Controlled framing, or enclosing the cosmetics in a mesh or fabric “lightbox,” creates a “tent” over the cosmetics. This helps you control reflections, glare, and shadows. 4. Maintain visual consistency Every background and prop you choose affects how a product photographs. A matte skincare tube looks different against warm marble versus a neutral, cool white surface. For glossy lip products and similar cosmetics, busy or textured backgrounds pull customers’ eyes away from the item. Uniform styling saves production time. It also helps shoppers make decisions. When the only variation between your product visuals is the items on display, your images are easier to compare and look more professional. To create that kind of cohesive visual experience, every variable has to stay fixed between the shots; for example, the same white background so texture shows up, or the same angle and lighting so a palette’s shade range looks accurate. For beauty brands managing thousands of shimmer palettes and lipstick SKUs, that is a serious production challenge. Photoroom’s Brand Kit and Batch mode tools address that challenge directly. Your brand kit centralizes your assets, such as logos, fonts, and colors, so you can apply them to every image. And with batch editing , you can apply the same background, lighting, retouching, and branding to up to 250 images at once. 5. Streamline post-production and editing Post-production is where a good photoshoot becomes a great catalog—but it’s also where many teams lose time. Raw images often need exposure tweaks, surface retouching, and color correction, so the visuals look just like the physical products. Beauty photo editing typically involves: Adjusting the composition: Straighten or realign the products to correct any drift in framing between shots. Refining the exposure: Lift shadows and recover details where they’re needed. Retouching the surfaces: Remove any blemishes on the images, such as dust, smudges, or fingerprints. Correcting colors: Match color tones and white balance across photos. Photoroom handles all these editing steps within the same app or web-based interface. You can cleanly isolate products with AI Background Remover , change colors with Recolor , then eliminate unwanted objects and imperfections with Magic Retouch . Plus, you can use Product Beautifier to correct local lighting issues and refine edges, maintaining better accuracy and consistency across your entire catalog. Most importantly, these features integrate with the rest of your production process. Instead of wasting time switching between tools, you can create, polish, optimize, and export or publish your product photos in the same place. 6. Optimize for e‑commerce marketplaces Marketplace image requirements are non-negotiable because non-compliant images get suppressed, reducing visibility and sales. Here’s how to prepare your cosmetics photography: High resolution: Details like shimmer finishes and fine textures show through in high-resolution photos. Most major platforms require images that are a minimum of 1,000 x 1,000 pixels. Consistent lighting and exposure: Images must match across your catalog. If one lipstick is brighter than the others, or some skincare products have shadows and some don’t, the results look unprofessional and can reduce trust in your brand. Clean background: Many marketplaces require listing images with pure white backgrounds and no props or borders. If you do use stylized backgrounds, keep them simple and standardized, so the focus stays on the beauty products. Search engine optimization (SEO): SEO elements , like descriptive file names and alt text, help your beauty product listings get indexed and discovered online. Correct sizing and formatting: Each marketplace has its own preferred image sizes and file types, along with other requirements like specific color modes or resolutions. With Photoroom, you can automatically apply all the right marketplace specs to your listing photos in bulk. Automate your beauty product production workflow with Photoroom Makeup product photoshoots that drive conversions require careful preparation and consistency across every SKU. Doing that manually is time-consuming; even perfectly executed photoshoots create bottlenecks when your team has thousands of images to edit. Photoroom offers an end-to-end solution for producing and editing beauty product visuals. You can generate new images or upload existing ones, then apply branding and styling consistently across 250 listing visuals at a time. AI tools automate background removal, enhance lighting and texture, and correctly format your images, so they’re listing-ready in no time. Download Photoroom from the App Store or Google Play , or use the web app to get started.

title: LiveRamp Expands Across Travel, Gaming, and More: Scaling the Trusted Network for AI-Powered Marketing
summary: Electronic Arts and Giphy among brands that joined the trusted data collaboration network
body_text: Electronic Arts and Giphy among brands that joined the trusted data collaboration network As AI and agentic workflows reshape the marketing landscape, the need for a trusted data foundation has never been higher. Over the past six months, LiveRamp has seen strong momentum with new clients across travel, gaming, retail, financial services, and more – alongside nine new partner integrations that further expanded the power and reach of the trusted LiveRamp network. Why Global Brands are Joining the LiveRamp Data Collaboration Network New additions, like Electronic Arts, underscore the strength and prestige of the brands choosing LiveRamp. At the same time, partner integrations with brands like Giphy highlight how LiveRamp is increasingly woven into the fabric of digital engagement and modern consumer expression. Together, these brands reflect why LiveRamp continues to be the partner of choice for organizations looking to collaborate responsibly in an AI-driven world. Existing customers are already demonstrating what this looks like in practice. Comcast , for example, works with LiveRamp to deliver spot-on measurement for faster optimization and smarter spending, and to develop clean room collaborations for scaling high-quality audiences and performance outcomes.
